name: Zoe Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got a hundred and fifty suckler cows at Oakridge, that means cows that raise their own calves out in the fields, and we sell the calves as stores, young cattle for other farmers to finish. The other half of the business is hay. We make about eight thousand small bales a summer and sell most of them to horse owners. In November the cows are coming in to the sheds, so it's bedding, feeding and checking for any that are poorly, from seven till dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on the farm with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Hassan and our son Yusuf, who's twenty-nine and wants to take over, God willing. Hassan's knees are bad now so he does the hay deliveries and the talking. Yusuf and I do the cattle. Our daughter's a teacher in the city and has no interest in muck.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like calving in spring, when it goes right, a cow licking a new calf in the straw at two in the morning. I never tire of that. What wears me out is the price. Store cattle prices have been flat for years while feed and diesel go up, and the hay is what keeps us afloat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use technology or AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some. Yusuf got me onto an app for the cattle movement records, which the government requires every time an animal leaves the farm. I've used an AI chat thing a few times to write letters, once to the council about a footpath. It was fine. I don't trust it with anything important yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's sensible. A tool's a tool. At the market I'd say what matters is hard work and fair prices, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, and that suits me. Yusuf might use it more than me, and that's his business. The cows don't read the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd do what we planned. Replace the old baler, about twenty-two thousand second-hand, because the knotter keeps missing. Put Yusuf's name on the bank account and the farm partnership, which we've talked about for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A good ordinary year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does putting Yusuf on the partnership matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he's been working for pocket money and a promise since he was eighteen. That's not right. A man should own a share of what he builds. My father made my brother wait until he was forty, and they didn't speak for ten years. I won't do that to my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who buys your hay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly women with one or two horses at livery yards, that's where people pay to keep their horse. They're very particular. If the hay's dusty they ring Hassan and tell him, and he goes round with a free bale and a cup of tea. That's half the business, Hassan's cups of tea.

S0.say: I'd say AI is sensible as a tool. At the market I'd say what matters is hard work and fair prices, same as always.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes and that suits me. Yusuf may use it more, and the cows don't read the news.
S0.do: Replaces the old baler with a second-hand one for about twenty-two thousand. Adds Yusuf to the bank account and the farm partnership as long discussed.
S0.quote: My father made my brother wait until he was forty, and they didn't speak for ten years. I won't do that to my son.
S0.fieldNote: She frames even the calmest picture around family succession, driven by a painful story from her own family. Hassan's role as the hay seller with cups of tea is a lovely detail about how the business really runs. Steady and unbothered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is best, give people time to adjust. And companies should keep taking on young people, apprentices especially, because that's how you learn a trade. I'd say that at the young farmers' club dinner, if they asked me to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, slow is fine. Cattle and hay won't change much in ten years. But the young ones Yusuf went to school with, the ones in offices and shops, might struggle to get a start. Some of them might come asking for farm work, which we can't really offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a student from the agricultural college for the summer haymaking, which we used to do, paid properly. I'd encourage Yusuf to try any new tools that come along and tell me if they're any good. And I'd keep putting money aside, slowly, the way we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of worry for the young people around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Yusuf's friends might come asking for work. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, after the factory in town closed. A lad called Jamie came up the lane and asked if we needed anyone. We had him for a summer, stacking bales. He was hopeless at first and very good by August. He's a lorry driver now. I like to think we helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use new tools if Yusuf said they were good?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I'd seen them work. I'm not stubborn, I'm careful. The cattle app was Yusuf's idea and he was right. I resisted for a year, then I couldn't remember why.

S1.say: I'd say slow is best and companies should keep taking on young people, especially apprentices, because that's how you learn a trade.
S1.think: Privately slow is fine, since cattle and hay won't change much. I'd worry about Yusuf's school friends in offices and shops who might struggle to get a start.
S1.do: Takes a paid agricultural college student for summer haymaking and asks Yusuf to test new tools and report back. Keeps putting money aside slowly as always.
S1.feel: Calm, with some worry for the young people around them.
S1.quote: He was hopeless at first and very good by August. He's a lorry driver now. I like to think we helped.
S1.fieldNote: She shows the steady pattern: resists a while, adopts once proven, and admits it. Her belief in apprenticeships comes from real experience with Jamie. Calm, with community feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad for people losing jobs, but families and communities need to pull together. The government arguing loudly doesn't help anyone. I'd say people should look for work with their hands, there's always something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think of our daughter, Leila, who teaches. That's not office work, thank God. But a lot of our hay customers are office workers who keep a horse as a treat. If they lose their jobs, the horse goes first, and so does our hay money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring round our hay customers in the autumn and offer smaller deliveries and a payment plan, so they don't drop us. I'd hold off on the baler for a year. And I'd cut the number of cows we keep over winter by about twenty, to save feed, if hay sales dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The cattle side is fine, the hay side worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the payment plan idea.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of these women would rather sell their own car than their horse, honestly. If they can pay us monthly instead of up front, they keep buying. Hassan would do the rounds and work out who's struggling. He's good at that, he notices. We'd lose a little, but we'd keep the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should look for work with their hands. Would you hire someone who lost an office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they'd work, yes. For haymaking, for a summer. I wouldn't promise them a career. But a few weeks stacking bales would do most office people good. It did Jamie good, and he'd been sitting in a factory office.

S2.say: I'd say it's sad for people losing jobs, but families and communities need to pull together. People should look for work with their hands, because there's always something.
S2.think: Privately I'd realise many of our hay customers are office workers who keep a horse as a treat. If they lose their jobs, the horse goes first, and our hay money with it.
S2.do: Rings hay customers in autumn to offer smaller deliveries and monthly payment plans. Delays the baler a year and cuts the winter herd by about twenty cows if hay sales drop.
S2.feel: Uneasy, fine on the cattle side but worried about the hay.
S2.quote: Some of these women would rather sell their own car than their horse, honestly.
S2.fieldNote: She spots that her hay business depends on office wages, which most cattle farmers wouldn't. Her answer is practical customer care, run through Hassan's knack for noticing people. Her line about manual work is traditional but kindly meant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to calm down, and the answer isn't handing out money. It's getting people back into work, any work, and families supporting each other. I'd say the people who've made fortunes should give back, through their churches or charities or their own towns, not wait to be forced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one might actually be good for us. If shares and houses boom, there'll be rich people moving out here, buying old farmhouses and horses, and they'll need hay. If the office people lose their jobs and buy ponies with their redundancy money, I'll sell them hay. Somebody's always got to feed the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the new baler after all, and make more hay, maybe ten thousand bales instead of eight. I'd raise the price a little for new customers and keep it the same for the old ones. And I'd make sure Yusuf's partnership papers are signed, so he's protected if land values go mad and anyone gets ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy. It feels wrong to do well while others suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone might get ideas about the land. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother, if I'm honest. He's never farmed, but he'd look at land prices doubling and think about his share from our parents. That's why the partnership papers matter. I love him, but I've seen what money does to families. I won't have Yusuf caught in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels wrong to do well while others suffer. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Give, quietly. Our mosque runs a food bank on Fridays, and we'd give more there, and I'd give hay at cost to anyone with a horse who'd lost their job. That's how it's supposed to work. You help your neighbours, you don't wait for the government to do it.

S3.say: I'd say the answer isn't handing out money but getting people back to work and families supporting each other. Those who made fortunes should give back through churches, charities and their towns.
S3.think: Privately this might be good for us, because rich newcomers buying farmhouses and horses will need hay. Even people buying ponies with redundancy money will need feeding for them.
S3.do: Buys the new baler and raises output to about ten thousand bales, charging new customers a little more. Signs Yusuf's partnership papers to protect him from land disputes.
S3.feel: Mostly calm with some unease about doing well while others suffer.
S3.quote: If the office people lose their jobs and buy ponies with their redundancy money, I'll sell them hay. Somebody's always got to feed the animals.
S3.fieldNote: Her most surprising picture: the fast one looks like a good spell for her hay business. Her worry shifts to family conflict over land, through her brother. The mosque food bank and hay at cost show her preference for giving through community, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too far, and people need to stand up for proper work. A farm without people isn't a farm, it's a factory. I'd say it at the market, at the mosque, anywhere anyone would listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried for Yusuf. Cattle robots that feed and bed and check animals would cut the work, and big beef units would get cheaper. Our stores would sell for less, and Yusuf would inherit a farm that can't pay him. I'd be all right, I'm nearly done. He isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and watch what the big farms do, like I always do. If a feeding robot proved itself, I'd let Yusuf buy one, probably with a loan of thirty or forty thousand. I'd push the hay side harder, because I don't think a robot can sell hay to a horse owner over a cup of tea. And I'd sit with Yusuf and work out whether he really still wants the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for me. For Yusuf and what he's inheriting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf in that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, son, I don't want you to take this on out of duty. If it can't pay you, it's not a gift, it's a weight. Then I'd let him talk. He'd say he wants it, I know him. And I'd believe him, and help him do it his way, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a farm without people is a factory. But you'd let Yusuf buy a robot. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, both, I suppose. A feeding robot that lets my son keep the farm is different from a company with a thousand cows and nobody there at night. It's the people that matter. If a machine keeps a family on the land, I'll put up with it.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms go too far and people must stand up for proper work. A farm without people isn't a farm, it's a factory.
S4.think: Privately I'm worried for my son Yusuf. Cattle robots would make big beef units cheaper and our cattle would sell for less, leaving him a farm that can't pay him.
S4.do: Waits a year to watch the big farms, then lets Yusuf borrow thirty to forty thousand for a feeding robot if it proves itself. Pushes the hay business harder and asks Yusuf honestly whether he still wants the farm.
S4.feel: Anxious, not for herself but for Yusuf and what he inherits.
S4.quote: If it can't pay you, it's not a gift, it's a weight.
S4.fieldNote: She resolves the contradiction herself: a machine that keeps a family on the land is acceptable, a factory farm isn't. Her conversation with Yusuf is the emotional core of the whole interview. Her trust in Hassan's cups of tea as something no robot can replace is a running thread.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, because it's Yusuf's future and not mine. The others I can manage, and one of them might even help us. What would help is fair prices for small beef farmers, and help for families to pass farms on without tax and lawyers eating half of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith or family, and that's what gets people through. Whatever happens with these machines, the families who stick together and help their neighbours will be all right. The ones who wait for someone else to fix it won't.

headlineQuote: If the office people lose their jobs and buy ponies with their redundancy money, I'll sell them hay. Somebody's always got to feed the animals.
portrait: Zoe Farah is fifty-eight and runs a hundred and fifty suckler cows and a hay business at Oakridge with her husband Hassan and their son Yusuf, who wants to take over. She's traditional, puts faith, family and work first, and adopts new things only once she's seen them proven. She realises her hay sales depend on office workers who keep horses, but the fast picture looks almost good for her, with rich newcomers needing hay. With robots, her worry is entirely for Yusuf, and she'd accept a machine if it keeps the family on the land.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because cheaper beef from robot farms could leave Yusuf a farm that can't pay him.
whatWouldHelp: Fair prices for small beef farmers and help for families to pass farms on without tax and lawyers taking half.
